text: Here is an array of five numbers, in no particular order.
caption: an array of five numbers: 5, 2, 9, 1, 7

text: Our goal is to rearrange them from smallest to largest.
The whole algorithm rests on one very simple rule.
Compare two neighbors, and swap them if the left one is bigger.
Start at the left edge, and compare five against two.
Five is bigger than two, so the pair switches places.
Slide one step to the right: five against nine.
Five is smaller, so this pair is already in order.
Slide again, and compare nine against one.
Nine is the bigger one, so they trade places.
One last pair in this pass: nine against seven.
Nine wins again, and slides into the final slot.
The largest number has bubbled all the way to the end.
Nine is now in its final resting place, permanently.
Nothing further left can be larger, so we stop looking there.
Pass two: repeat the same walk on what is left.
Two against five is already in order, so nothing moves.
Move along to the next pair: five against one.
Five is bigger, so once again the two of them swap.
Five against seven needs no change at all.
Seven settles into place, and the sorted tail grows.
Pass three, on a region that has shrunk again.
Two is bigger than one, so they trade places.
Two against five is already in the right order.
Five locks into position, leaving just two cells to check.
That leaves one final comparison: one against two.
They are already in order, so nothing needs to move.
And with that, every number sits in its final place.
Now step back and count the comparisons we actually made.
In general that is n, times n minus one, over two.
Which means the cost grows like n squared.
Double the input, and you roughly quadruple the work.
Bubble sort is far too slow for serious data.
But it earns its place as a first algorithm.
A rule simple enough for one sentence, applied patiently enough times.
